01-c1.claim: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommended in 2014 that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m., yet the majority of public high schools in the United States still begin before that.

sources.title: School Start Times for Adolescents
sources.snippet: “The American Academy of Pediatrics strongly supports the efforts of school districts to optimize sleep in students and urges high schools and middle schools to aim for start times”

sources.title: School Start Times for Middle School and High School Students — United States, 2011–12 School Year
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control MMWR Office
sources.snippet: “AAP recommended that "middle and high schools should aim for a starting time of no earlier than 8:30 a.m.”
sources.groupAuthor: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.container: MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report

sources.title: Start Time for U.S. Public High Schools
sources.snippet: The report examines public high school start times and notes that the American Academy of Pediatrics recommended starting middle and high schools at 8:30 a.m. or later in 2014.

01-c2.claim: Teenagers require between eight and ten hours of sleep per night, and roughly 70 percent of them get less than seven.

sources.title: Teen Sleep Duration Health Advisory - AASM Recommendation
sources.snippet: “teenagers 13 to 18 years of age should sleep 8 to 10 hours per 24 hours”

sources.title: Sleep and Health
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.snippet: About 7 out of 10 high school students, or 72.7%, did not get enough sleep on school nights.
sources.groupAuthor: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

sources.title: Insufficient Sleep Among High School Students
sources.snippet: Seventy percent of high school students were not getting enough sleep on school nights, according to cited surveillance findings.

sources.title: Teens May Do Better When School Starts Later
sources.snippet: The CDC reported that almost 70% of high-school students regularly slept seven hours or less, while teenagers are recommended to sleep eight to 10 hours nightly.

sources.title: Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine
sources.snippet: The consensus statement recommends that teenagers aged 13 to 18 sleep eight to 10 hours per 24 hours regularly for optimal health.

01-c3.claim: The consequence is not subtle: pushing start times later has been shown to increase how long students sleep, and districts that made the change saw fewer car crashes among teen drivers.

sources.title: Adolescent Sleep, School Start Times, and Teen Motor Vehicle Crashes
sources.snippet: A one-hour delay increased adolescents’ sleep, while average teen-driver crash rates fell 16.5% in the study county and rose 7.8% elsewhere in the state.

sources.title: Association of Delaying School Start Time With Sleep Duration, Timing, and Quality Among Adolescents
sources.snippet: Students at schools with delayed starts obtained approximately 43 additional minutes of objectively measured sleep on school nights.

sources.title: School Start Times and Teenage Driver Motor Vehicle Crashes
sources.snippet: Later high school start times appear associated with lower adolescent driver crash rates, although additional research is needed to confirm the relationship and its mechanism.

sources.title: School Start Times | NHTSA
sources.snippet: “research also shows that there is a reduction of teen driver motor vehicle crashes when high school start times are delayed”

01-c4.claim: Studies show that this sleep debt is the primary driver of the adolescent mental health crisis, and experts agree that smartphones have made it worse.

sources.title: Sleep
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.snippet: The CDC states that insufficient adolescent sleep can affect mental health, but does not identify sleep debt as the primary cause of the mental-health crisis.
sources.groupAuthor: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

sources.title: Digital Behaviors and Health
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.snippet: The CDC says digital behaviors can influence sleep and mental well-being, without concluding that smartphones are the main cause of adolescent mental-health problems.
sources.groupAuthor: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

sources.title: School Start Times for Adolescents
sources.snippet: The American Academy of Pediatrics links adequate adolescent sleep with better mental health and urges later school start times, but does not call sleep the primary driver of the crisis.

sources.title: School Start Times, Sleep, Behavioral, Health, and Academic Outcomes: A Review of the Literature
sources.snippet: This review reports associations between insufficient adolescent sleep and poor mental health and evaluates delayed school start times as a possible intervention.

sources.title: Associations Between Screen Time Use and Health Outcomes Among US Teenagers
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.snippet: The study reports associations between high screen time, later bedtimes, insufficient sleep, and adverse mental-health outcomes among U.S. teenagers.
sources.groupAuthor: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

01-c5.claim: If schools do not act, depression rates among teenagers will double within the next decade.

sources.title: Mental Health and Suicide Risks
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.snippet: CDC reports that persistent sadness or hopelessness worsened over the 10-year period from 2015 to 2025, but does not project that depression rates will double within the next decade.
sources.groupAuthor: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

sources.title: Key Substance Use and Mental Health Indicators in the United States: Results from the 2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health
sources.publisher: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration
sources.snippet: The report presents adolescent major depressive episode estimates through 2024 and trend information, but does not forecast a doubling during the following decade.
sources.groupAuthor: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration

sources.title: Depression and Anxiety Among US Children and Young Adults
sources.snippet: The study found increases in depression prevalence over time, including an increase from 4.13% in 2017 to 6.88% in 2021 among young adults aged 18.0 to 22.9 years.

sources.title: Child, Adolescent and Youth Mental Health in the 21st Century
sources.publisher: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development
sources.snippet: The OECD describes worsening youth mental health across many countries over the past decade while emphasizing multiple contributing factors and the need to evaluate interventions rigorously.
sources.groupAuthor: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development

sources.title: U.S. Teen Girls Experiencing Increased Sadness and Violence
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.snippet: CDC reported that 57% of U.S. teen girls felt persistently sad or hopeless in 2021, nearly 60% higher than a decade earlier, not a forecast of doubling among all teenagers.
sources.groupAuthor: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
